claims.text: The initial alloy has titanium and nickel as primary constituents, with every constituent between 5 and 35 at%.
The initial titanium- and nickel-primary alloy forms a simple solid-solution phase.
Adding 5–10 at% Nb and applying a tailored heat treatment will produce Nb-rich precipitates in the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy.
Nb atoms will partition during heat treatment to form precipitates.
The resulting Nb-rich precipitates will be nanoscale, fine, and well dispersed.
The Nb-rich nano-precipitates will remain thermally stable at elevated temperature.
Nb provides solid-solution or precipitate strengthening in the proposed alloy.
The Nb-rich precipitates will obstruct or pin dislocations at high temperatures.
Dislocation obstruction by the precipitates will increase elevated-temperature yield strength.
Dislocation obstruction by the precipitates will improve elevated-temperature creep resistance.
The Nb-containing alloy will have higher yield strength than the Nb-free alloy at 800–1000 °C.
The Nb-containing alloy will have lower creep strain rate or otherwise greater creep resistance than the Nb-free alloy at elevated temperature.
If the proposed mechanism is active, the strength increase will be approximately 15–30%.
Coarse phases formed during heat treatment would be deleterious.
The magnitude of improvement will depend on Nb content, processing conditions, and testing temperature.

contradictions.description: The baseline field defines the control as lacking both Nb and the same heat treatment, whereas the experiment says that an identical heat treatment will be applied to the Nb-free and Nb-added samples. These are materially different controls.

The hypothesis attributes improvement to adding Nb, but the stated baseline also omits the heat treatment included in the intervention. Under that baseline, any observed difference could not be assigned specifically to Nb.
